quote: There’s also a lot of hype, that AI will create evil robots with super-intelligence. That’s an unnecessary distraction ... There could be a race of killer robots in the far future, but I don’t work on not turning AI evil today
claim_summary: Calls the hype about evil super-intelligent robots an unnecessary distraction; says killer robots could exist in the far future but are not worth working on today, like overpopulation on Mars.
definition_note: "evil robots with super-intelligence" (his words for the feared capability); not defined
notes: secondhand; basis: "There could be a race of killer robots in the far future"; The Register (Chris Williams), report of his keynote at Nvidia's GPU Technology Conference, San Jose, published the same day (byline 2015-03-19, talk "on Thursday"). Quote read on The Register page. Quote Investigator (2020-10-04) transcribes the same passage from the conference video, so the words are close to primary, but no transcript of the talk itself was read. Judgment calls: the target is set to superintelligence because he is answering fears of "evil robots with super-intelligence"; "killer robots" alone does not name a capability, so ambiguous: yes (target). "could" with "in the far future" is a hedge, so uncertain (ruling 10). Agency left unexpressed: "I can't productively work on" it now is about present tractability, not whether the outcome can be shaped. Earliest statement in his record.

quote: I think that hundreds of years from now if people invent a technology that we haven’t heard of yet, maybe a computer could turn evil. But the future is so uncertain. I don’t know what’s going to happen five years from now.
claim_summary: Asked for the best reason to worry about destructive AI, says perhaps hundreds of years from now, with technology not yet invented, a computer could turn evil, but the future is too uncertain to say.
timeline_text: hundreds of years from now ... maybe
notes: basis: "maybe a computer could turn evil"; Wired (Caleb Garling), Skype interview, page dated 2015-05-05 in its metadata; the live wired.com page is now 404, read in the Wayback Machine snapshot of 2017-02-05. Interviewer's question: "What’s the most valid reason that we should be worried about destructive artificial intelligence?" Next sentences: the Mars analogy. The URL is under wired.com/brandlab (Wired's branded-content section), but it carries Garling's byline and is a Q&A with direct answers. Judgment calls: target superintelligence with ambiguous: yes (target) for the same reason as ng-2015-01, since "turn evil" names no capability. "hundreds of years" gives no number, so timeline_year is left blank.

quote: Worrying about killer robots today is like worrying about overpopulation on Mars.
claim_summary: At the Structure Data conference, repeats that worrying about killer robots today is like worrying about overpopulation on Mars.
notes: secondhand; Fortune (Stacey Higginbotham), dated 2016-03-09, report of his talk at the Structure Data conference in San Francisco "on Wednesday" (2016-03-09). Quote read on the Fortune page. The reporter paraphrases him as admitting robots might some day be intelligent enough to worry about but "aren't even close to capable today". That is the reporter's words, so it is not coded: endorsement stays unexpressed. Judgment calls: the target is set to superintelligence and ambiguous: yes (target), as in ng-2015-01; the Mars analogy implies a distant capability without saying so, so timeline is qualitative with text "today". Borderline as a qualifying statement; recorded so as not to skip it.

quote: A→B is far from the sentient robots that science fiction has promised us. Human intelligence also does much more than A→B.
claim_summary: Writes that today's AI (supervised learning from input A to output B) is far from science fiction's sentient robots, and that human intelligence does much more.
definition_note: "sentient robots that science fiction has promised us", contrasted with human intelligence
notes: Harvard Business Review article under his byline, datePublished 2016-11-09 in the page metadata; full text read in the article body embedded in the page (fetched with curl, since r.jina.ai showed only the paywall). Article says "If a typical person can do a mental task with less than one second of thought, we can probably automate it using AI either now or in the near future" (narrow tasks, not coded). Judgment call: "far from" and "much more than" deny that current systems match human intelligence, so present_capability disputed; nothing is said about the future, so endorsement unexpressed (ruling 9).

quote: Since the early days of AI, people have wondered whether AI can ever be conscious or feel emotions. Even though an artificial general intelligence may be centuries away, these are important questions.
claim_summary: Says artificial general intelligence may be centuries away, though questions about AI consciousness and emotion still matter.
notes: basis: "may be centuries away"; The Batch issue 26, his weekly letter ("Dear friends"), published 2020-02-12 per the issue page. The letter is mainly about whether an AI can love or be conscious, which he calls philosophical questions; frame_primary is timeline because the only claim about AGI itself is its timing, and other_concern (consciousness) is present. "may" with "centuries" is a hedge, so uncertain (ruling 10); no number of centuries, so timeline_year blank.

quote: I continue to believe that some combination of learning algorithms, likely yet to be invented, will get us there someday.
claim_summary: Says he still believes some combination of learning algorithms, probably not yet invented, will eventually reach artificial general intelligence.
definition_note: "a system that can learn to perform any mental task that a typical human can" (same letter)
notes: basis: "will get us there someday"; The Batch issue 135 letter, published 2022-03-09. "there" refers to AGI, named in the sentences before. Same letter: building AGI is "one of the grandest challenges of our time"; "Obviously, AGI would have extraordinary value"; he co-organized a NIPS 2005 workshop on human-level AI; ends "If you dream of making progress toward AGI yourself, I encourage you to keep dreaming!" Consequences, affect and agency are taken from those lines in the same letter, outside the stored quote; judgment call, so coding_confidence would be medium for those fields.

quote: Many people think that AI means AGI (artificial general intelligence), which remains far away. They don’t understand how deeply AI is already embedded in society.
claim_summary: Says many people equate AI with AGI, which remains far away, and do not see how much AI is already in use.
notes: The Batch issue 140 letter, published 2022-04-13. Judgment call: "remains far away" says AGI is not here and is distant, but unlike "decades away" it names no unit of time, so it is coded like altman-2015-03 ("a long, long way"): present_capability disputed, endorsement unexpressed, with the words kept in timeline_text.

quote: Similarly, recent progress on LLMs and image generation models has reignited speculation about artificial general intelligence (AGI). Generative AI is very exciting! Nonetheless, today’s models are far from AGI.
claim_summary: Says progress in language and image models has revived talk of AGI, but today's models are far from it.
definition_note: Wikipedia definition quoted in the same letter: "the ability of an intelligent agent to understand or learn any intellectual task that human beings or other animals can"
notes: The Batch issue 189 letter, published 2023-03-22. Affect: "Generative AI is very exciting!" is an explicit cue, though about generative AI rather than AGI. Same letter, later: "While AGI may be part of an indeterminate future, we have amazing capabilities today" (a hedge, not coded here because it is a separate passage; it would be uncertain).

quote: it seems unlikely that a 6-month pause in our decades-long journey toward AGI would have much useful impact.
claim_summary: Argues against the proposed six-month pause on frontier models, saying a pause would matter little in a decades-long journey toward AGI.
notes: The Batch issue 192 letter, published 2023-04-12, on the March 2023 pause letter (he and Yann LeCun discussed it online). Ambiguous field: endorsement and timeline. "decades-long journey" could mean the journey has lasted decades or will take decades; it presupposes AGI as the destination but does not say it will be reached, so endorsement unexpressed. Same letter calls loss of control of "runaway AI (or AGI, or even superintelligent systems)" an unlikely scenario (consequences, not coded as a capability claim).

quote: I believe that most people, including me, currently think of AGI as AI that can carry out any intellectual task that a human can. With this definition, I think we’re still at least decades away from AGI.
claim_summary: Defines AGI as AI that can do any intellectual task a human can, and says that by this definition it is still at least decades away.
definition_note: AI that can carry out any intellectual task that a human can
notes: basis: "I think we’re still at least decades away from AGI"; The Batch issue 232 letter, published 2024-01-17, on defining sentience and AGI. A14 ruling 11 ("decades away") and A15 ruling 5 ("at least") both point to accepts. No number of decades is given, so timeline_year is left blank and the row is qualitative rather than a range; the lower_bound tag is not used because it needs a year. Same letter warns against redefining AGI with a lower bar to declare success.

quote: Even though nontechnical pundits talk about “the race to AGI” as if AGI were a discrete technology to be invented, the reality is that AI technology will progress continuously ... If a company or nation declares that it has achieved AGI, I expect that declaration to be less a technology milestone than a marketing milestone.
claim_summary: Says AI will progress continuously with no single finish line, and that any claim to have achieved AGI will be more marketing than a technical milestone.
definition_note: not a discrete technology; no single finish line
notes: The Batch issue 312 letter, published 2025-07-30, on the US-China AI competition. The "..." drops "and there is no single finish line ." (a link in the original). Judgment call: he does not say AGI will never come, only that a declaration of it would be a marketing claim; present_capability disputed reads that as disputing any such claim, endorsement unexpressed.

quote: Modern AI is a general purpose technology that is enabling many applications, but AI that can do any intellectual tasks that a human can (a popular definition for AGI) is still decades away or longer.
claim_summary: Says AI that can do any intellectual task a human can is still decades away or longer.
definition_note: AI that can do any intellectual tasks that a human can
notes: basis: "is still decades away or longer"; The Batch issue 327 letter, published 2025-11-12, on AI hype ("AI is general, but not that general"). "decades away" is accepts with a qualitative timeline (A14 ruling 11); "still" disputes present capability.

quote: We shouldn’t buy into the inaccurate hype that LLMs are a path to AGI in just a few years, but we also shouldn’t buy into the opposite, also inaccurate hype that they are only demoware.
claim_summary: Calls it inaccurate hype that large language models are a path to AGI within a few years.
notes: basis: "inaccurate hype that LLMs are a path to AGI in just a few years"; The Batch issue 332 letter, published 2025-12-17. Ambiguous field: endorsement. The claim rejects both a route (language models) and a near date; under A15 ruling 4 a route claim alone would be unexpressed, but here the timing ("in just a few years") is what he calls inaccurate, so coded rejects for that horizon only. No not_by tag because "a few years" gives no year (2025 + a few). He does not say whether AGI comes later (see ng-2025-02, "decades away or longer").

quote: “AGI” has turned into a term of hype rather than a term with a precise meaning. A reasonable definition of AGI is AI that can do any intellectual task that a human can. When businesses hype up that they might achieve AGI within a few quarters, they usually try to justify these statements by setting a much lower bar.
claim_summary: Proposes a 'Turing-AGI Test'; says AGI has become a hype term, defines it as AI that can do any intellectual task a human can, and says claims of AGI within a few quarters rest on a lower bar.
definition_note: AI that can do any intellectual task that a human can; tested by doing a work task as well as a skilled human (Turing-AGI Test)
notes: The Batch issue 334 (New Year issue) letter, published 2026-01-02; the panel verification's latest statement for him. Same letter: CEOs sometimes assume "AI will be more capable in 1-2 years than any likely reality"; hype risks a bubble; "If we run a Turing-AGI Test competition and every AI system falls short, that will be a good thing!" Consequence (economic, harmful: a bubble) and agency (a test can recalibrate expectations) come from the same letter, outside the stored quote. No position on when AGI arrives, so endorsement unexpressed.
